articles.title: Building umbral: an FX agent that refuses on purpose
articles.excerpt: I built an agent that converts USDT into Argentine pesos, Brazilian reais and a few other LatAm currencies on Celo, and is designed to say no most of the time. This is the long version: why refusals b…
articles.body: I built an agent that converts USDT into Argentine pesos, Brazilian reais and a few other LatAm currencies on Celo, and is designed to say no most of the time. This is the long version: why refusals beat conversions, how the money path works without CELO in the wallet, what the ledger actually guarantees, and where it all falls short because I never funded the wallet. The brief and the constraint that shaped everything The brief for "Agents on Open Rails" was money that moves without a human in the loop, on open rails. Celo has the useful pieces: stablecoins with real depth, a firm quote RFQ venue in Textile, x402 for payments, ERC-8004 for identity, ERC-8021 for attribution, and CIP-64 so a transaction can pay its fee in a stablecoin.

articles.title: The Code Never Reached the Phone: What SilentAir Actually Teaches
articles.excerpt: Most accounts treat a texted code as proof that the right person holds the right phone. A report published on November 11 by Enea, a Stockholm-based telecom software and security company, describes a…
articles.body: Most accounts treat a texted code as proof that the right person holds the right phone. A report published on November 11 by Enea, a Stockholm-based telecom software and security company, describes a threat actor that sits inside mobile operator networks and arranges for those texts to arrive somewhere else first. For some targeted subscribers, Enea observed two-factor authentication codes being intercepted immediately after the interception was switched on. The actor is new, the mechanism is old, and the lesson is architectural: a code delivered by SMS is only as trustworthy as the least trustworthy operator in the chain that carries it. That chain is longer than most people assume.
articles.author: Damiano

articles.title: How I built a 3ms self-hosted AI drift proxy in Python (and wiped deleted prompts from SQLite WAL files)
articles.excerpt: If you run LLMs in production—whether OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or self-hosted Ollama/vLLM—you have probably been burned by silent model drift. An upstream provider tweaks quantization or safety filt…
articles.body: If you run LLMs in production—whether OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or self-hosted Ollama/vLLM—you have probably been burned by silent model drift . An upstream provider tweaks quantization or safety filters overnight, refusal rates jump, or an update subtly breaks edge-case prompts without any announcement. Most observability platforms solve this in two frustrating ways: They require shipping all your raw customer prompts to a third-party cloud. They rely on static threshold alerts (like alerting whenever response length changes), which spam false alarms whenever a model is naturally verbose.

articles.title: Opportunity Discovery: A Practical Guide for When You're Stuck
articles.excerpt: Opportunity Discovery: A Practical Guide for When You're Stuck The Problem in Concrete Terms You have the capacity to build. You have time, maybe some savings, perhaps a skill set that people pay for.…
articles.body: Opportunity Discovery: A Practical Guide for When You're Stuck The Problem in Concrete Terms You have the capacity to build. You have time, maybe some savings, perhaps a skill set that people pay for. What you don't have is a clear signal on what to build. Every idea feels either too small to matter, too crowded to enter, or too vague to validate. You've read about "finding your niche" and "scratching your own itch," but your own itches are either already solved by existing tools or too idiosyncratic to support a business. You've tried listing problems you encounter daily, but the list either runs dry after five items or balloons into hundreds of minor annoyances with no clear path to revenue.

articles.title: Musk Said Send Grok a Photo of Your Card. Would You Do It?
articles.excerpt: On October 10th, Elon Musk told people to take a picture of their credit card and drop it into the Grok Bot chat so it could find a deal and order it. His proof the next day was a $241.34 Lego Star Wa…
articles.body: On October 10th, Elon Musk told people to take a picture of their credit card and drop it into the Grok Bot chat so it could find a deal and order it. His proof the next day was a $241.34 Lego Star Wars order, and the screenshot showed two addresses, an email, an order number and the last digits of his Amex. Nobody has shown whether that order actually used a card photo, or whether he approved the charge. Grok Bot's own shopping feature doesn't need a photo at all. It pays through Stripe's Link wallet: you approve each purchase, and the bot gets a one-time card or token instead of your real card. We also cover the xAI privacy-policy line that disappeared the day after his post, Visa's warning about fake stores built to fool AI shoppers, and the simple rule for letting an AI shop for you.

articles.title: Ten coding-agent deletions, traced to the shell command that ran
articles.excerpt: Between September and November this year, several incidents were made public in which a coding agent deleted user files or killed unrelated processes. They came from Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity an…
articles.body: Between September and November this year, several incidents were made public in which a coding agent deleted user files or killed unrelated processes. They came from Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity and opencode alike. Most write-ups stop at "the agent ran rm -rf", but when you look at the actual commands, the agent almost never set out to delete something broad. In most cases a command meant to remove one narrow folder ended up pointing somewhere else because of shell evaluation order, quote handling, the return value of a path tool, or a link. This post covers only the cases where the executed command can be confirmed from the original source (GitHub issues, Reddit posts and their attached screenshots).

articles.title: This Week In Space podcast: Episode 236 — Alienspotting
articles.excerpt: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space, Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize.
articles.body: On Episode 236 of This Week In Space , Tariq Malik and Rod Pyle are joined by Mikhail Tikhonov to talk about how life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. When we think of extraterrestrials, our minds generally go from the latex-suited bipedal aliens seen in Star Trek and Star Wars to more exotic critters in sci-fi movies. Scientists think in terms of carbon-based microbial life and other lower life forms. But some researchers, such as Tikhonov from Washington University, suggest that life can take more unusual forms, ones we might not even recognize. He further suggests a new definition of life: something that takes in and transforms energy and replicates. His ideas radically expand our notions of alien life and how it might be recognized.

articles.title: Why did Starship Flight 15 booster abort 'chopsticks' landing catch? SpaceX still investigating (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13) during the Starship Flight 15 test.
articles.body: SpaceX is looking into why its latest Starship megarocket test flight missed the first of two planned landings on Friday (Nov. 13), triggering an automatic abort that destroyed the booster. The giant Starship rocket , a massive two-stage vehicle that's the largest launcher on Earth, soared into orbit from SpaceX's Starbase in South Texas on Friday on the company's ambitious Flight 15 test flight. The goal: To land both the Super Heavy first stage and the Ship upper stage, for the first full Starship recovery — and the first complete recovery of an orbital launch system in history. The Super Heavy stage, called Booster 22, came back to Earth mere minutes after liftoff as planned.
articles.author: Tariq Malik

articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 14, 1969: NASA's Apollo 12 astronauts launch to the moon on a 'pinpoint landing' lunar mission
articles.excerpt: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 astronauts launched to the moon. Here's why it mattered.
articles.body: On Nov. 14, 1969, the Apollo 12 mission launched to the moon. This was the second moon landing of the Apollo program. The two astronauts on board were Pete Conrad , commander, and Alan Bean , the lunar module pilot. Astronaut Richard Gordon , the command module pilot, stayed in the command module and orbited the moon while his crewmates went to the surface. The astronauts made a pinpoint landing in a lunar mare called the Ocean of Storms. The previous moon mission, Apollo 11 , drifted far from the planned landing zone. But Apollo 12 landed close to a scientific target. That target was a robotic lander called Surveyor 3 . Scientists wanted to look at Surveyor 3 to see how well the spacecraft lasted on the moon since it landed there more than two years earlier.
articles.author: Hanneke Weitering

articles.title: Watch SpaceX will attempt its 1st-ever 'chopsticks' Starship landing catch of a rocket from orbit today (livestream)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX plans to catch the upper stage of its Starship megarocket at the launch pad today (Nov. 14), and you can watch the unprecedented action live.
articles.body: SpaceX plans to catch the upper stage of its Starship megarocket for the first time ever today (Nov. 14), and you can watch the action live. Starship launched on its 15th test flight on Friday evening (Nov. 13), rising into the sky from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. The mission plan called for bringing both of the vehicle's stages back to Starbase and catching them with the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — an unprecedented total recovery of an orbital rocket . That didn't happen, however; SpaceX diverted Starship's Super Heavy booster to a controlled splashdown in the Gulf of Mexico 6.5 minutes after launch. (SpaceX said later that a guidance and navigaton issue during its descent triggered and automatic abort .

articles.title: See Jupiter and Mars make a spectacular close approach overnight Nov. 15-16
articles.excerpt: The red planet Mars will shine a little over 1 degree from Jupiter on the night of Nov. 15-16.
articles.body: Heads up stargazers! Mars meets Jupiter for a spectacular rendezvous in the heart of the constellation Leo on the night of Nov. 15-16, and they won't be this close again until July 2029. Jupiter and Mars will appear a little over 1 degree from each other as they rise over the eastern horizon around midnight for viewers in the U.S., as the blue-white light of the main-sequence star Regulus glows below, according to In-The-Sky . It's all a trick of perspective, but spectacular nonetheless. In reality Mars and Jupiter are separated by a gulf of over 368 million miles (592 million kilometers), while the light from Regulus has travelled for some 79 light-years before reaching Earth .

articles.title: SpaceX launches Starship on ambitious 22-hour Flight 15 test, but aborts booster 'chopsticks' catch (video)
articles.excerpt: SpaceX's Starship megarocket reached orbit today (Nov. 13) during its 15th test flight, but the company scrapped a plan to catch the vehicle's massive booster back at the launch site.
articles.body: STARBASE, Texas — SpaceX launched the 15th test flight of its massive Starship rocket today (Nov. 13) and is preparing the vehicle's upper stage for its first-ever return to the launch site in less than 24 hours. Flight 15 lifted off from SpaceX 's Starbase facility here in South Texas at 5:47 p.m. ET (2247 GMT; 4:47 p.m. local Texas time). The towering Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage cleared the tower without incident and climbed into the skies under more than 18 million pounds of thrust from the booster's 33 Raptor 3 engines. The flight continued nominally through its initial ascent, with the successful execution of Super Heavy's main engine cutoff and Ship's subsequent hot-staging — firing its own Raptors during separation from the booster — about 2.5 minutes after launch.
